The Daodejing is usually read as 81 chapters in order. Chapter 1, chapter 2, and on to chapter 81, each one a small poem about water, valleys, and not doing too much.

That order is real — the received text has it — but it is not the only structure in the book. This edition regroups the 81 chapters into five movements:

- 根 (root) — what the Dao is. 15 chapters, anchored on ch. 25, "道法自然".
- 动 (motion) — how it moves. 11 chapters, anchored on ch. 40, "反者道之动".
- 生 (generation) — how the ten thousand things come out. 14 chapters, anchored on ch. 42, "道生一".
- 落 (decline) — how order slides down. 24 chapters, anchored on ch. 38, "失道而后德".
- 还 (return) — how to go back. 17 chapters, anchored on ch. 81, "为而不争".

Two chapters carry the whole spine: 25 asks what it is, 40 asks how it moves. Everything else hangs off one of the two.

## Why regroup at all

The received order is not random, but it is also not a syllabus. Reading straight through, you meet the same idea at chapter 1, again at 14, again at 25, again at 39, without being told they are the same idea. The book looks repetitive because the reading order hides the argument.

Regrouping does not add anything to the text. It only makes the spine visible: every chapter gets assigned to the question it actually answers, and chapters that answer the same question sit together.

It also makes the book checkable. If a chapter is in 落, it should be talking about decline — the loss of 道 into 德 into 仁 into 义 into 礼. If it isn't, either the assignment is wrong or the chapter is doing two things at once. That is a testable claim, which is more than most reading orders offer.

## What each movement is doing

**根** establishes that 道 is not a being. It is the frame before things take shape — the same 无 from chapter 1, looked at as a source rather than a lens. Chapter 25's "道法自然" is not "nature is divine"; it is "the Dao models itself on what is so of itself," which is a statement about not having an outside reference.

**动** is the hinge. "反者道之动" — the movement of the Dao is reversal. Things that reach an extreme turn; what is bent becomes straight; what is full empties. This is not a moral lesson about humility. It is a description of how a system with a boundary behaves.

**生** is generation: one, two, three, the ten thousand things. The interesting part is not the arithmetic but the claim that division is how the Dao produces anything at all — unity that stays unity produces nothing.

**落** is the longest section, and the least comfortable. Once 道 is lost, 德 appears; once 德 is lost, 仁; then 义; then 礼. Each stage is a repair for the stage before, and each is a step further from the source. Chapter 38 is placed at the head of this movement, not because it is early in the text, but because it names the mechanism.

**还** is the return. Not back to a previous state, which is impossible, but back to a position where the mechanism is visible again. Chapter 81 closes with 为而不争 — act, don't contest — which is the whole book's answer reduced to four characters.

## What this fixes

Three persistent misreadings come from reading the chapters in a flat line:

1. **"无为" read as passivity.** In 动 and 还, 无为 is consistently paired with action: 为而不争, 无为而无不为. It is a mode of acting, not an absence of action.
2. **"柔弱胜刚强" read as advice for the weak.** In 生 and 落, softness is a property of systems that survive, not a tactic for losers.
3. **"绝圣弃智" read as anti-intellectualism.** In 落, it is a statement about what happens when virtue is turned into a credential — the chapter is aimed at the label, not at intelligence.

None of this is a new doctrine. It is what the text says when the chapters are allowed to answer the questions they were written for.

## The book

81 chapters, 3 supplementary essays, 11 appendices, 88.6 万 non-blank characters. Every chapter runs eight layers: base text, notes, character exegesis, cross-text comparison, Confucian calibration, common misreadings, a closing line, and sources. Base texts are kept in parallel where 帛书 A, 帛书 B, and the Wang Bi text disagree.
